edges.description: Cold-evoked mitochondrial ROS activates RhoA/ROCK signaling in arteriolar vascular smooth muscle cells.
RhoA/ROCK-mediated filamin engagement and actin cytoskeletal rearrangement mobilize Golgi/ER alpha-2C adrenoceptors to the VSMC plasma membrane and potentiate cold-induced vasoconstriction.
Postsynaptic alpha-2C adrenoceptor activation drives calcium influx and smooth muscle contraction in digital artery walls.
Exaggerated cold-induced digital arterial vasoconstriction produces episodic triphasic Raynaud attacks.
Digital arteriolar spasm acutely restricts cutaneous and acral blood flow.
Sympathetic activation of overexpressed arterial alpha-2A adrenoceptors promotes VSMC calcium influx and vasoconstriction.
Arterial alpha-2A adrenoceptor overexpression lowers the threshold for catecholamine-evoked digital vasospasm.
Enhanced alpha-2A-mediated arteriolar constriction reduces acral perfusion during sympathetic activation.
Calcium-dependent vascular smooth muscle contraction executes acute digital arterial vasospasm.
Sustained smooth muscle contraction narrows digital lumen diameter and restricts acral blood flow.
Downstream microvascular stasis during sustained vasospasm leads to venous deoxygenation and transient digital cyanosis.
Vasospastic hypoperfusion and neurovascular nociceptor activation provoke burning digital pain.
Acute digital nerve hypoperfusion during vasospasm causes transient numbness and paresthesia.
Estrogen-GPER1 signaling upregulates alpha-2C-AR abundance and cold-induced contractile responsiveness.
Putative IRX1-mediated impairment of prostaglandin/bradykinin vasodilatory responsiveness increases susceptibility to vasospastic episodes.
Blunted vasodilatory counterbalance prolongs digital hypoperfusion during vasoconstrictive stimuli.
Loss of endothelial nitric oxide and prostacyclin promotes local platelet activation and impaired fibrinolysis.
Impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilation and excess endothelin-1 prolong digital hypoperfusion.
Structural endothelial injury, failed angiogenesis, and intimal fibroproliferation in secondary RP cause ischemic digital ulcers.
Sympathetic norepinephrine release activates cold-mobilized postsynaptic alpha-2C adrenoceptors on digital VSMCs.
Sympathetic catecholamine release engages overexpressed arterial alpha-2A adrenoceptors during cold or emotional stress.
Neurovascular imbalance between sympathetic vasoconstriction and CGRP-mediated vasodilation triggers episodic digital color changes.
Platelet aggregation, impaired fibrinolysis, and hyperviscosity reduce digital microvascular perfusion.
Sluggish hyperviscous microvascular blood flow deepens digital venous deoxygenation.
Recurrent ischemia-reperfusion oxidant stress damages microvascular endothelium and depletes nitric oxide bioavailability.
Cumulative ischemia-reperfusion oxidative injury promotes irreversible digital tissue necrosis in severe secondary RP.
Repeated vasospastic digital ischemia followed by reperfusion hyperemia generates vascular oxidant stress and endothelial injury.

Local cooling is directly sensed by vascular smooth muscle mitochondria acting as thermosensors, triggering reactive oxygen species release that initiates RhoA/ROCK activation and alpha-2C adrenoceptor mobilization.

Acute emotional stress activates central autonomic outflow and peripheral sympathetic adrenergic discharge to digital resistance vessels and arteriovenous anastomoses, triggering catecholamine-mediated vasospasm even in thermoneutral environments.

meta.association: Genome-wide significant risk locus at 10q25.2 (lead variant rs7090046, OR 1.26, p < 9.6 x 10^-27) colocalizing with higher arterial ADRA2A cis-eQTL expression in both overall and stringently defined primary Raynaud phenomenon.

evidence.reference_title: ADRA2A and IRX1 are putative risk genes for Raynaud's phenomenon.
evidence.snippet: We prioritized ADRA2A (rs7090046, odds ratio (OR) per allele: 1.26; 95%-CI: 1.20-1.31; p < 9.6 × 10-27) and IRX1 (rs12653958, OR: 1.17; 95%-CI: 1.12-1.22, p < 4.8 × 10-13) as candidate causal genes through integration of gene expression in disease relevant tissues.

nodes.description: Common germline regulatory risk variants at the ADRA2A locus increase arterial expression of alpha-2A adrenoceptors, sensitizing small arteries and arterioles to sympathetic catecholamine-induced vasoconstriction even under thermoneutral conditions.

evidence.reference_title: ADRA2A and IRX1 are putative risk genes for Raynaud's phenomenon.
evidence.snippet: Variant rs1343449 is a reported gene expression quantitative trait locus (cis-eQTL) for ADRA2A in artery tissue and statistical colocalization confirmed a shared genetic signal with RP with high confidence (tibial artery, posterior probability (PP) > 96%; Fig. 2), with the RP risk-increasing A-allele of rs7090046 being associated with higher ADRA2A expression (beta = 0.28, p = 1.0 × 10−9).

evidence.reference_title: ADRA2A and IRX1 are putative risk genes for Raynaud's phenomenon.
evidence.snippet: Through integration with gene expression data, we demonstrated that the strongest locus likely acts via increased expression of α2A-adrenoreceptors in arterial tissue, augmenting the current concept of predominantly α2C-adrenoreceptors mediating the vasospasms seen in RP patients

nodes.description: Cold-induced RhoA/ROCK-dependent translocation of alpha-2C adrenoceptors (ADRA2C) from the Golgi/ER to the plasma membrane and receptor activation in microvascular smooth muscle cells mediate local cooling-induced vasoconstriction of digital arteries and arterioles.

evidence.reference_title: Raynaud syndrome.

evidence.reference_title: Cold responses and hormonal echoes: a comprehensive view of Raynaud's vascular dysfunction.

evidence.reference_title: Pathogenesis of Raynaud's phenomenon.
evidence.snippet: Neural abnormalities include deficiency of the vasodilator calcitonin gene-related peptide (released from sensory afferents), alpha(2)-adrenoreceptor activation (possibly with up-regulation of the normally 'silent' alpha(2C)-adrenoreceptor) and a central nervous system component.

nodes.description: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine, amlodipine) are first-line pharmacotherapy. They reduce frequency and severity of vasospastic attacks by inhibiting L-type calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle cells.

evidence.reference_title: Raynaud's Phenomenon: A Current Update on Pathogenesis, Diagnostic Workup, and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (CCBs), such as nifedipine, are commonly used for vasodilation.

evidence.reference_title: Calcium channel blockers for primary and secondary Raynaud's phenomenon.
evidence.snippet: CCBs (especially the dihydropyridine class) may be useful in reducing the frequency, duration, severity of attacks, pain and disability associated with Raynaud's phenomenon.

nodes.description: Behavioral modification including wearing warm gloves, avoiding cold exposure, stress management, and hand warming. First-line non-pharmacological management for all patients with Raynaud phenomenon.

evidence.reference_title: Raynaud syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Most patients with RS can be managed conservatively, with avoidance of cold exposure or hand warming.

nodes.description: Cold ambient temperature or direct contact with cold objects is the primary trigger for vasospastic episodes, initiating VSMC mitochondrial ROS release and downstream RhoA/ROCK-dependent alpha-2C adrenoceptor vasoconstriction.

evidence.reference_title: Cold responses and hormonal echoes: a comprehensive view of Raynaud's vascular dysfunction.

nodes.description: Transient blue discoloration of affected digits following the initial pallor phase of a vasospastic attack, reflecting venous blood deoxygenation prior to reperfusion hyperemia.

evidence.reference_title: Cold responses and hormonal echoes: a comprehensive view of Raynaud's vascular dysfunction.

evidence.reference_title: Raynaud's phenomenon: from molecular pathogenesis to therapy.

nodes.description: Impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilation with reduced nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin bioavailability and increased production of endothelin-1 (ET-1). The imbalance between vasoconstrictors and vasodilators favors persistent vasoconstriction, platelet activation, and intimal proliferation. In secondary RP associated with systemic sclerosis, endothelial damage leads to defective angiogenesis, endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and progressive capillary loss.

evidence.reference_title: Endothelial Dysfunction in Systemic Sclerosis
evidence.snippet: Endothelial damage and activation occur early, possibly triggered by various infectious agents and autoantibodies. Endothelial dysfunction, along with defects in endothelial progenitor cells, leads to defective angiogenesis and vasculogenesis.

evidence.reference_title: Recent Insights into Cellular and Molecular Mechanisms of Defective Angiogenesis in Systemic Sclerosis
evidence.snippet: once damaged, endothelial cells can be dysfunctionally activated, thus becoming unable to undergo angiogenesis and promoting perivascular inflammation. They can also undergo apoptosis, transdifferentiate into profibrotic myofibroblasts

nodes.description: Bosentan blocks endothelin-1 receptor signaling and is effective in preventing new digital ulcers in patients with systemic sclerosis-associated secondary Raynaud phenomenon and multiple digital ulcers.

evidence.reference_title: Raynaud's Phenomenon: A Current Update on Pathogenesis, Diagnostic Workup, and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: Bosentan, an endothelin-1 receptor antagonist, has shown effectiveness in treating and preventing digital ulcers, especially in patients with multiple ulcers.

evidence.reference_title: Cold responses and hormonal echoes: a comprehensive view of Raynaud's vascular dysfunction.

nodes.description: Common germline risk alleles at 5p15.33 increase expression of the homeobox transcription factor IRX1 in skeletal muscle and tibial artery, putatively altering transcriptional regulation of prostaglandin (PTGER1/PTGS2) and bradykinin (BDKRB2) signaling pathways and blunting microvascular vasodilation.

evidence.reference_title: ADRA2A and IRX1 are putative risk genes for Raynaud's phenomenon.
evidence.snippet: Increased expression of the transcription factor IRX1 in muscle, and possibly arterial tissue, may further alter genes involved in prostaglandin and/or bradykinin sensing and production, providing a putative second novel mechanism identified in our genetic study.

nodes.description: Platelet activation and release of thromboxane A2 and serotonin contribute to vasospasm. Altered coagulation and fibrinolysis pathways and increased blood viscosity further impair microvascular flow during episodes. Gene ontology analysis identifies enrichment in negative regulation of fibrinolysis and complement/coagulation cascades among RP-associated genes.

evidence.reference_title: Pathogenesis of Raynaud's phenomenon.

nodes.description: Episodic vasospasm of digital arteries triggered by cold or stress, producing the characteristic triphasic color change: pallor (ischemia), cyanosis (deoxygenation), and erythema (reperfusion). This is the defining clinical feature.

evidence.reference_title: Raynaud syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Raynaud syndrome (RS) was first described by the French physician Maurice Raynaud in 1862 with the characteristic tricolor change featuring pallor (ischemic phase), cyanosis (deoxygenation phase), and erythema (reperfusion phase) induced by cold or stress.

evidence.reference_title: Raynaud's phenomenon: from molecular pathogenesis to therapy.

nodes.description: Surgical sympathectomy can be used for severe, refractory Raynaud phenomenon to interrupt sympathetic adrenergic vasoconstriction, though long-term effectiveness is uncertain.

evidence.snippet: sympathectomy surgery can be used to control RP symptoms. However, botulinum toxin injections require repeated administration, and sympathectomy's long-term effectiveness is uncertain.

nodes.description: Increased sympathetic adrenergic outflow to digital resistance vessels and arteriovenous anastomoses, together with reduced sensory-nerve vasodilator calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release, disrupts neurovascular tone and triggers vasospasm in response to cold or emotional stress.

nodes.description: Voltage-gated L-type calcium channel opening in digital arterial and arteriolar vascular smooth muscle cells drives intracellular calcium influx and myosin-light-chain-dependent contractile vasospasm, providing the direct pharmacological target of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.
